ta-no.name: Taíno
ta-no.summary: Indigenous people of the West Indies, part of the Arawak group, who lived in agricultural societies led by caciques and were the first New World peoples encountered by non-Norse Europeans.

acadia.name: Acadia
acadia.summary: A French colony in northeastern North America, covering parts of the Maritime provinces, Gaspé and Maine, contested repeatedly by Britain until it was ceded in 1710 and renamed Nova Scotia.

nixtamalization.name: Nixtamalization
nixtamalization.summary: A process of soaking and cooking maize in an alkaline solution such as limewater, which improves its nutrition and flavor and makes it possible to form dough (masa).

apalachee.name: Apalachee
apalachee.summary: An Indigenous Muskogean-speaking people of Florida's Panhandle who first met Spanish explorers in 1528 and abandoned their homeland by 1704 after devastating warfare.

jamestown.name: Jamestown, Virginia
jamestown.summary: First permanent English settlement in the Americas, founded in the Colony of Virginia in 1607; it served as Virginia's colonial capital until 1699.

united-empire-loyalist.name: United Empire Loyalists
united-empire-loyalist.summary: An honorific title given to American Loyalists who resettled in British North America during and after the American Revolution, mainly in Nova Scotia and Quebec, shaping future English-speaking Canada.

upper-canada.name: Upper Canada
upper-canada.summary: A British colonial province established in 1791 covering modern southern Ontario, settled largely by Loyalist refugees after the American Revolution.

gullah.name: Gullah
gullah.summary: An African American ethnic group of the coastal Carolinas, Georgia and Florida, descended from enslaved West and Central Africans, with a distinctive creole culture and language.

south-carolina-lowcountry.name: Lowcountry
south-carolina-lowcountry.summary: Coastal region of South Carolina once built on slave-grown rice and indigo, home today to historic cities and the Gullah/Geechee community.

new-amsterdam.name: New Amsterdam
new-amsterdam.summary: The 17th-century Dutch settlement at the tip of Manhattan and capital of New Netherland, seized by the English in 1664 and renamed New York.

recife.name: Recife
recife.summary: A major port city on Brazil's northeastern coast, founded in 1537; it was known as Mauritsstad when it served as capital of the 17th-century Dutch colony of New Holland.

wolastoqiyik.name: Maliseet
wolastoqiyik.summary: An Algonquian-speaking First Nation, the Indigenous people of the Saint John River valley across present-day New Brunswick, Quebec and Maine.

mi-kmaq.name: Mi'kmaq
mi-kmaq.summary: An Indigenous people of Canada's Atlantic Provinces and Maine, part of the Wabanaki confederation, who signed Peace and Friendship Treaties with the British Crown through the 18th century.

penobscot.name: Penobscot
penobscot.summary: An Indigenous people of the Northeastern Woodlands, now a federally recognized tribe in Maine and part of the Wabanaki Confederacy.

st-augustine-florida.name: St. Augustine, Florida
st-augustine-florida.summary: A city in northeastern Florida founded by Spanish settlers in 1565, the oldest continuously inhabited European-founded settlement in what is now the contiguous United States.

anastasia-island.name: Anastasia Island
anastasia-island.summary: A barrier island off northeast Florida near St. Augustine, about 14 miles long, separated from the mainland by the Matanzas River and home to the Spanish colonial-era Fort Matanzas.

coquina.name: Coquina
coquina.summary: A sedimentary rock made of shell and mollusk fragments, formed in high-energy coastal environments and historically quarried as a building stone.

francisco-v-zquez-de-coronado.name: Francisco Vázquez de Coronado
francisco-v-zquez-de-coronado.summary: Spanish conquistador and explorer (1510–1554) who led an expedition from Mexico to Kansas in 1540–1542 seeking the mythical Cities of Gold; his party made the first European sightings of the Grand Canyon.

pueblo-peoples.name: Pueblo peoples
pueblo-peoples.summary: Native Americans of the southwestern United States sharing agricultural, material and religious traditions, descended from the Ancestral Puebloans and including the Taos, Zuni and Hopi communities.

castillo-de-san-marcos.name: Castillo de San Marcos
castillo-de-san-marcos.summary: The oldest masonry fort in the continental United States, built in St. Augustine, Florida, with construction beginning in 1672 under Spanish rule.

fort-matanzas-national-monument.name: Fort Matanzas
fort-matanzas-national-monument.summary: A Spanish fort built in 1740 on Florida's Atlantic coast, now a US national monument since 1924.

santa-fe-de-nuevo-m-xico.name: Santa Fe de Nuevo México
santa-fe-de-nuevo-m-xico.summary: A province of the Spanish Empire and later Mexico covering the area that became New Mexico, with its capital moved to Santa Fe in 1610.

massachusetts-bay-colony.name: Massachusetts Bay Colony
massachusetts-bay-colony.summary: An English colony (1628 to 1691) on the coast of North America around Boston and Salem, settled mostly by Puritans; it was New England's first slave-holding colony.

st-paul-s-chapel.name: St. Paul's Chapel
st-paul-s-chapel.summary: The oldest surviving church building in Manhattan, built in 1766 in Georgian style, nicknamed 'The Little Chapel That Stood' after surviving the September 11 attacks.

georgian-architecture.name: Georgian architecture
georgian-architecture.summary: A set of architectural styles used across Britain from 1714 to 1830, named after the Hanoverian kings George I to IV and marked by symmetry and classical proportion.

cabinet-of-curiosities.name: Cabinets of curiosities
cabinet-of-curiosities.summary: Encyclopedic private collections of natural, historical and artistic objects that emerged in 16th-century Europe, precursors to modern museums.

san-francisco-de-as-s-mission-church.name: Mission San Francisco de Asís
san-francisco-de-as-s-mission-church.summary: 18th-century Spanish colonial Catholic church in Ranchos de Taos, New Mexico, built between 1772 and 1816 and long a popular subject for artists.
san-francisco-de-as-s-mission-church.source_title: San Francisco de Asís Mission Church

ranchos-de-taos-new-mexico.name: Ranchos de Taos, New Mexico
ranchos-de-taos-new-mexico.summary: A small community in Taos County, New Mexico, home to the historic San Francisco de Asis Mission Church.

pueblo-revival-architecture.name: Pueblo Revival architecture
pueblo-revival-architecture.summary: A regional architectural style of the southwestern United States, developed in the early 20th century and most popular in the 1920s-30s, drawing on traditional Pueblo building, Spanish missions and Territorial style.

mission-san-xavier-del-bac.name: Mission San Xavier del Bac
mission-san-xavier-del-bac.summary: A historic Spanish Catholic mission near Tucson, Arizona, founded in 1692, rebuilt in the 1780s–90s, and now the oldest European structure in Arizona.

churrigueresque.name: Churrigueresque
churrigueresque.summary: A Spanish Baroque style of elaborate sculptural ornament that emerged in Spain in the late 17th century and was used until about 1750, marked by extreme, florid decorative detailing on building façades.

estipite.name: Estipite
estipite.summary: A pilaster shaped like an inverted pyramid or obelisk, used in Mannerist and Baroque buildings and later a signature feature of Spain's ornate Churrigueresque style.

peter-harrison-architect.name: Peter Harrison
peter-harrison-architect.summary: English-born architect (1716–1775) who emigrated to New England and introduced the Palladian style to the Thirteen Colonies.

redwood-library-and-athenaeum.name: Redwood Library and Athenaeum
redwood-library-and-athenaeum.summary: A subscription library and museum founded in 1747 in Newport, Rhode Island, whose 1750 building was the first library built for that purpose in the United States.

quillwork.name: Quillwork
quillwork.summary: A form of textile decoration traditionally made by Indigenous peoples of North America using dyed porcupine quills, and occasionally bird-feather quills.

birchbark-biting.name: Birchbark biting
birchbark-biting.summary: An Indigenous artform in which artists bite folded pieces of birch bark into intricate designs, practiced by Anishinaabeg, Cree, and other Algonquian peoples of North America.

george-washington.name: George Washington
george-washington.summary: First president of the United States (1789–1797) and commander of the Continental Army, credited as a Founding Father for leading American victory in the Revolutionary War.

continental-army.name: Continental Army
continental-army.summary: The colonial force created in 1775 by the Second Continental Congress to fight Britain in the Revolutionary War, commanded by George Washington until its 1784 disbandment.

treaty-of-paris-1783.name: Treaty of Paris (1783)
treaty-of-paris-1783.summary: 1783 treaty between Britain and the United States that officially ended the War of American Independence and recognized the Thirteen Colonies as free and independent.

little-turtle.name: Little Turtle
little-turtle.summary: A chief (Sagamore) of the Miami people, c. 1747-1812, who led a confederation of Native American warriors to major victories against U.S. forces in the 1790s Northwest Indian Wars, including St. Clair's defeat.

blue-jacket.name: Blue Jacket
blue-jacket.summary: A Shawnee war chief (about 1743–1810) who fought to defend Shawnee lands in the Ohio Country and led a multi-tribal alliance against the early United States in the Northwest Indian War.

arthur-st-clair.name: Arthur St. Clair
arthur-st-clair.summary: A Scottish-born American military officer and politician (1737–1818) who served as President of the Continental Congress and suffered a major defeat against Native American forces in 1791.

josiah-harmar.name: Josiah Harmar
josiah-harmar.summary: US Army officer (1753–1813) who served in the Revolutionary War and was the Army's senior officer for over six years during the Northwest Indian War.

northwest-indian-war.name: Northwest Indian War
northwest-indian-war.summary: A conflict from 1785 to 1795 between the United States and a confederation of Native American peoples for control of the Northwest Territory, considered the first American Indian War.

beaver-wars.name: Beaver Wars
beaver-wars.summary: A series of 17th-century conflicts in North America between the Dutch- and English-backed Haudenosaunee and French-backed Indigenous nations, partly over the fur trade.

haudenosaunee.name: Haudenosaunee
haudenosaunee.summary: A confederacy of Iroquoian-speaking peoples in northeast North America, originally five (later six) nations united under the Great Law of Peace, called the Iroquois by Europeans.

wendat-people.name: Wendat
wendat-people.summary: A confederacy of Indigenous nations, also known as the Huron, who were one of the principal powers of the Great Lakes region until dispersed by the Haudenosaunee in the 1650s.

siege-of-yorktown.name: Siege of Yorktown
siege-of-yorktown.summary: The decisive 1781 battle in which George Washington's Continental Army and French forces defeated the British under Cornwallis, effectively ending the American Revolutionary War.

george-iii.name: George III
george-iii.summary: King of Great Britain and Ireland from 1760 to 1820, whose reign saw victory over France in the Seven Years' War but the loss of Britain's American colonies.

battles-of-lexington-and-concord.name: Battles of Lexington and Concord
battles-of-lexington-and-concord.summary: The first major clashes between British troops and Patriot militia, fought on 19 April 1775 in Massachusetts, marking the start of the American Revolutionary War.

second-continental-congress.name: Second Continental Congress
second-continental-congress.summary: The 1775 to 1781 assembly of delegates from the Thirteen Colonies that led the American Revolution, raised the Continental Army, and adopted the Declaration of Independence in 1776.

battle-of-fallen-timbers.name: Battle of Fallen Timbers
battle-of-fallen-timbers.summary: The final battle of the Northwest Indian War, fought on 20 August 1794 near Ohio's Maumee River, where U.S. forces defeated a Native American confederacy, opening the way for the Treaty of Greenville.

maumee-river.name: Maumee River
maumee-river.summary: A river running from northeastern Indiana into northwestern Ohio and Lake Erie, near which the 1794 Battle of Fallen Timbers was fought.

anthony-wayne.name: Anthony Wayne
anthony-wayne.summary: American soldier and Founding Father (1745–1796) nicknamed 'Mad Anthony,' who led U.S. forces to victory in the Northwest Indian War after service in the Revolutionary War.

legion-of-the-united-states.name: Legion of the United States
legion-of-the-united-states.summary: A reorganized US Army force active from 1792 to 1796 under Anthony Wayne, known for its 1794 victory at Fallen Timbers, later renamed the Army of the United States.

pocahontas.name: Pocahontas
pocahontas.summary: Powhatan woman, daughter of paramount chief Wahunsenacawh, captured by English colonists in 1613 and later married Jamestown planter John Rolfe.

samuel-argall.name: Samuel Argall
samuel-argall.summary: An English sea captain and Deputy-Governor of Virginia who, in 1613, captured Pocahontas and held her hostage to pressure the Powhatan Confederacy.

powhatan-native-american-leader.name: Powhatan
powhatan-native-american-leader.summary: Leader (c. 1547 to c. 1618) of the Powhatan Confederacy of Algonquian-speaking peoples in Tidewater Virginia, and father of Pocahontas; led the main resistance the English colonists faced after landing at Jamestown in 1607.

anglo-powhatan-wars.name: First Anglo-Powhatan War
anglo-powhatan-wars.summary: The first of three wars, starting in 1609 between Virginia's English colonists and the Powhatan Confederacy, ending with a 1614 peace settlement.

john-rolfe.name: John Rolfe
john-rolfe.summary: English explorer and tobacco farmer (c.1585–1622) who introduced a sweeter tobacco strain to Virginia and married Pocahontas, boosting the colony's economy.

queen-anne-s-war.name: Queen Anne's War
queen-anne-s-war.summary: 1702–1713 North American colonial conflict between Britain, France and Spain, forming the American theater of the War of the Spanish Succession.

war-of-the-spanish-succession.name: War of the Spanish Succession
war-of-the-spanish-succession.summary: An 1701–1714 European conflict sparked by the childless death of Charles II of Spain, pitting France's Philip of Anjou against Austria's Archduke Charles over control of the Spanish Empire.

siege-of-port-royal-1710.name: Siege of Port Royal
siege-of-port-royal-1710.summary: A 1710 British siege that captured the Acadian capital, Port Royal, from the French, beginning permanent British control of the region and its renaming as Nova Scotia.

battles-of-saratoga.name: Battles of Saratoga
battles-of-saratoga.summary: Two battles fought in September and October 1777 near Saratoga, New York, ending in a decisive American victory and British surrender that persuaded France to join the war as an American ally.

treaty-of-alliance-1778.name: Franco-American Alliance
treaty-of-alliance-1778.summary: A 1778 defensive alliance between France and the United States, signed in Paris by King Louis XVI's delegates and the Continental Congress, marking America's formal entry onto the world stage.

george-germain-1st-viscount-sackville.name: George Germain
george-germain-1st-viscount-sackville.summary: British Secretary of State for the Colonies from 1775 to 1782, widely blamed as the chief architect of Britain's failed strategy in the American War of Independence.

john-montagu-4th-earl-of-sandwich.name: Earl of Sandwich
john-montagu-4th-earl-of-sandwich.summary: British statesman (1718–1792) who held offices including First Lord of the Admiralty and Postmaster General; also credited with inventing the sandwich.

treaty-of-greenville.name: Treaty of Greenville
treaty-of-greenville.summary: Signed by General Anthony Wayne in August 1795 after the Battle of Fallen Timbers, it ended the Northwest Indian War and began annual U.S. payments of goods to the tribes.

jacques-ren-de-brisay-marquis-de-denonvi.name: Denonville
jacques-ren-de-brisay-marquis-de-denonvi.summary: Governor General of New France from 1685 to 1689 who led a 1687 campaign against the Seneca during the conflict with the Iroquois known as the Beaver Wars.
jacques-ren-de-brisay-marquis-de-denonvi.source_title: Jacques-René de Brisay, Marquis de Denonville

fort-frontenac.name: Fort Frontenac
fort-frontenac.summary: A French trading post and fort built in 1673 where the St. Lawrence River leaves Lake Ontario, on the site of present-day Kingston, Ontario, named for New France's governor.

lachine-massacre.name: Lachine massacre
lachine-massacre.summary: A surprise attack by 1,500 Mohawk warriors on the small French settlement of Lachine near Montreal in August 1689, part of the Beaver Wars, that killed around 24 people.

james-wilkinson.name: James Wilkinson
james-wilkinson.summary: American army officer and politician (1757–1825) later revealed as a paid Spanish spy despite serving as the U.S. Army's senior officer and Louisiana's first governor.

miami-people.name: Miami
miami-people.summary: An Indigenous, Algonquian-speaking people of the Great Lakes region who historically lived in what is now Indiana, Ohio and Michigan, mostly displaced to Indian Territory by 1846.

wea.name: Wea
wea.summary: A Native American tribe originally of western Indiana, closely related to the Miami; their descendants today form part of the Peoria Tribe of Indians of Oklahoma.

phillis-wheatley.name: Phillis Wheatley
phillis-wheatley.summary: American poet (c. 1753–1784) considered the first African-American author of a published book of poetry; born in West Africa, she was enslaved as a child and gained fame in England and the colonies.

poems-on-various-subjects-religious-and-.name: Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral
poems-on-various-subjects-religious-and-.summary: A 1773 collection of 39 poems by Phillis Wheatley, the first African-American woman to publish a book.
poems-on-various-subjects-religious-and-.source_title: Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral

olaudah-equiano.name: Olaudah Equiano
olaudah-equiano.summary: A formerly enslaved writer whose 1789 autobiography helped fuel Britain's abolitionist movement and the eventual Slave Trade Act of 1807.

the-interesting-narrative-of-the-life-of.name: The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano
the-interesting-narrative-of-the-life-of.summary: The 1789 autobiography of Olaudah Equiano describing his enslavement and path to freedom, one of the earliest and most influential works on the slave trade.
the-interesting-narrative-of-the-life-of.source_title: The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano

jupiter-hammon.name: Jupiter Hammon
jupiter-hammon.summary: Enslaved American writer, 1711 to about 1806, whose 1761 poem made him the first published African American poet in North America; he also preached against slavery.

cotton-mather.name: Cotton Mather
cotton-mather.summary: Puritan minister, naturalist and historian in colonial New England (1663-1728), remembered for defending the Salem witch trials and for his history Magnalia Christi Americana.

isaac-newton.name: Isaac Newton
isaac-newton.summary: English mathematician and physicist (1642–1727) whose 1687 Principia established the laws of motion and universal gravitation, founding classical mechanics.

john-winthrop.name: John Winthrop
john-winthrop.summary: English Puritan lawyer (1588–1649) and leading figure in founding the Massachusetts Bay Colony, who led the first large wave of colonists in 1630 and served as governor for 12 of its first 20 years.

william-bradford-governor.name: William Bradford
william-bradford-governor.summary: English Pilgrim Separatist who sailed to Plymouth Colony on the Mayflower in 1620, signed the Mayflower Compact, and served intermittently as Governor of Plymouth Colony for about 30 years between 1621 and 1657.

william-hill-brown.name: William Hill Brown
william-hill-brown.summary: American novelist (1765–1793), author of The Power of Sympathy (1789), usually considered the first American novel.

the-power-of-sympathy.name: The Power of Sympathy
the-power-of-sympathy.summary: 1789 American epistolary novel by William Hill Brown, widely considered the first American novel, warning against seduction and urging women's moral education and rational thinking.

benjamin-franklin.name: Benjamin Franklin
benjamin-franklin.summary: American polymath, printer and Founding Father (1706–1790) who signed the Declaration of Independence and served as the first postmaster general.

thomas-paine.name: Thomas Paine
thomas-paine.summary: An English-born American Founding Father whose pamphlets Common Sense and The American Crisis helped inspire the push for independence from Britain.

thomas-jefferson.name: Thomas Jefferson
thomas-jefferson.summary: Founding Father and third U.S. president (1801–1809) who wrote the Declaration of Independence and shaped Jeffersonian democracy, while enslaving over 600 people.

cadwallader-colden.name: Cadwallader Colden
cadwallader-colden.summary: An Irish-born physician, scientist and colonial administrator who served as governor of New York from 1760 to 1762 and again from 1763 to 1765.

carl-linnaeus.name: Carl Linnaeus
carl-linnaeus.summary: Swedish biologist and physician (1707–1778) who formalized binomial nomenclature, the modern system of naming organisms, and is known as the father of modern taxonomy.

the-autobiography-of-benjamin-franklin.name: The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin
the-autobiography-of-benjamin-franklin.summary: Benjamin Franklin's own unfinished account of his life, written between 1771 and 1790, and one of the most famous and influential autobiographies ever written.

zabdiel-boylston.name: Zabdiel Boylston
zabdiel-boylston.summary: Boston physician (1679–1766) credited with several American firsts, including the first smallpox inoculations in North America.

american-philosophical-society.name: American Philosophical Society
american-philosophical-society.summary: A scholarly society founded in Philadelphia in 1743 by Benjamin Franklin to promote research in the humanities and sciences; it remains active with about 1,000 elected members.

john-winthrop-the-younger.name: John Winthrop the Younger
john-winthrop-the-younger.summary: English-born physician, colonial administrator and alchemist (1606–1676) who was an early governor of the Connecticut Colony and helped unify its settlements and secure a royal charter.

royal-society.name: Royal Society
royal-society.summary: The United Kingdom's national academy of sciences, founded in 1660 and granted a royal charter by Charles II; the oldest continuously existing scientific academy in the world.

benjamin-banneker.name: Benjamin Banneker
benjamin-banneker.summary: American naturalist, mathematician, astronomer and almanac author (1731–1806), largely self-taught, who helped survey the original borders of Washington, D.C.

david-rittenhouse.name: David Rittenhouse
david-rittenhouse.summary: American astronomer, inventor, clockmaker and public official (1732–1796) who became the first director of the United States Mint.

charles-mason.name: Charles Mason
charles-mason.summary: English surveyor and astronomer (1728–1786) who, with Jeremiah Dixon, surveyed the Mason–Dixon line marking the borders between Maryland, Pennsylvania and Delaware from 1763 to 1767.

jeremiah-dixon.name: Jeremiah Dixon
jeremiah-dixon.summary: An English surveyor and astronomer (1733–1779) best known for surveying the Mason–Dixon line with Charles Mason, which came to mark borders between Maryland, Pennsylvania and Delaware.

george-i-of-great-britain.name: George I
george-i-of-great-britain.summary: First British monarch of the House of Hanover, reigning from 1714 until 1727, during a period when real power increasingly shifted to a prime minister-led cabinet.

magellanic-premium.name: Magellanic Premium
magellanic-premium.summary: A prize established in 1786 for major contributions to navigation, astronomy, or natural philosophy, awarded by the American Philosophical Society.

charles-ii-of-england.name: Charles II of England
charles-ii-of-england.summary: King of Scotland from 1649 and of England, Scotland and Ireland from 1660 until 1685, restored to the throne after years of exile following the English Civil War.

brood-x.name: Brood X
brood-x.summary: One of 15 broods of periodical cicadas that emerge regularly across the eastern United States, also called the Great Eastern Brood.

massospora-cicadina.name: Massospora cicadina
massospora-cicadina.summary: A fungal pathogen that infects only 13- and 17-year periodical cicadas, forming a spore 'plug' at the abdomen that causes infertility and death.

united-states-mint.name: United States Mint
united-states-mint.summary: The U.S. Treasury bureau producing the nation's coinage since its founding in Philadelphia in 1792, one of two federal agencies that make physical money.

treaty-of-paris-1763.name: Treaty of Paris (1763)
treaty-of-paris-1763.summary: 1763 treaty ending the Seven Years' War, under which Britain gained most of France's territory in North America.

french-and-indian-war.name: French and Indian War
french-and-indian-war.summary: A 1754–1763 conflict in North America between Britain and France and their Indigenous allies, generally considered part of the global Seven Years' War.

new-france.name: New France
new-france.summary: The territory France colonized in North America from 1534 to 1763, spanning from Newfoundland to the Canadian Prairies and including Canada, Acadia and Louisiana.

peace-of-utrecht.name: Peace of Utrecht
peace-of-utrecht.summary: A series of treaties, 1713 to 1715, ending the War of the Spanish Succession by letting Philip V keep the Spanish throne while renouncing any claim to the French one.

new-netherland.name: New Netherland
new-netherland.summary: A Dutch colony on the East Coast of North America (1614 to 1674), stretching from Delaware to Cape Cod, with settlements that became New York, New Jersey, Delaware and Connecticut.

pilgrims-plymouth-colony.name: Pilgrims
pilgrims-plymouth-colony.summary: English Separatist settlers who sailed on the Mayflower and founded Plymouth Colony in 1620 after fleeing religious persecution.

plymouth-colony.name: Plymouth Colony
plymouth-colony.summary: First permanent English colony in New England, founded in 1620 by the Pilgrims and linked to the American tradition of Thanksgiving.

james-oglethorpe.name: James Oglethorpe
james-oglethorpe.summary: British army officer and social reformer (1696–1785) who founded the Province of Georgia in 1732 as a refuge for debtors, banning slavery there.

northwestern-confederacy.name: Northwestern Confederacy
northwestern-confederacy.summary: A loose confederacy of Native American peoples in the Great Lakes region, formed after the American Revolutionary War to resist United States expansion.

tecumseh.name: Tecumseh
tecumseh.summary: Shawnee chief (1768–1813) who built a multi-tribal confederacy to resist American expansion, dying in battle during the War of 1812 and becoming a folk hero across several cultures.

war-of-jenkins-ear.name: War of Jenkins' Ear
war-of-jenkins-ear.summary: An 1739–1748 war between Britain and Spain, mostly fought in New Granada and the Caribbean, named after a British captain whose ear was allegedly cut off by a Spanish coast guard captain.

king-george-s-war.name: King George's War
king-george-s-war.summary: A 1744–1748 conflict in British North America that was part of the War of the Austrian Succession, ending with the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle, which restored the French fortress of Louisbourg.

samuel-johnson-american-educator.name: Samuel Johnson
samuel-johnson-american-educator.summary: Clergyman, educator, linguist, and philosopher in colonial America (1696-1772) who founded and was the first president of King's College, later Columbia University, a key figure of the American Enlightenment.

jonathan-edwards-theologian.name: Jonathan Edwards
jonathan-edwards-theologian.summary: American revivalist preacher, philosopher and Congregationalist theologian (1703–1758) who helped shape the First Great Awakening and is regarded as one of America's most important philosophical theologians.

junto-club.name: The Junto
junto-club.summary: A club for mutual self-improvement founded by Benjamin Franklin in Philadelphia in 1727, where members debated morals, politics and natural philosophy.

anne-hutchinson.name: Anne Hutchinson
anne-hutchinson.summary: English-born religious figure at the center of the Antinomian Controversy that split the Massachusetts Bay Colony in 1636–1638; tried and banished, she was later killed in a massacre after her household moved to New Netherland.

john-cotton-minister.name: John Cotton
john-cotton-minister.summary: English-born Puritan clergyman (1585–1652) considered the leading minister and theologian of the Massachusetts Bay Colony.

antinomian-controversy.name: Antinomian Controversy
antinomian-controversy.summary: A religious and political conflict in the Massachusetts Bay Colony from 1636 to 1638 pitting most ministers and magistrates against Free Grace advocates like Anne Hutchinson.

longhouse-religion.name: Longhouse Religion
longhouse-religion.summary: A religious movement founded in 1797 or 1799 by the Seneca prophet Handsome Lake, blending older Haudenosaunee traditions with some Christian influence.

handsome-lake.name: Handsome Lake
handsome-lake.summary: A Seneca religious leader and prophet who revived traditional Haudenosaunee religion after colonization's disruption, blending it with a revised code still practiced as the 'Code of Handsome Lake'; he lived 1735–1815.

seneca-people.name: Seneca
seneca-people.summary: An Iroquoian-speaking Indigenous nation that lived south of Lake Ontario and formed the westernmost of the Six Nations of the Haudenosaunee, known as 'Keepers of the Western Door.'

wakan-tanka.name: Wakan Tanka
wakan-tanka.summary: The Lakota term for the sacred or divine, often translated 'Great Spirit' or 'Great Mystery,' describing a power or holiness (wakan) believed to reside in everything.

midewiwin.name: Midewiwin
midewiwin.summary: A religious society, also called the Grand Medicine Society, of Indigenous peoples of the Great Lakes and nearby regions, keeping birch bark scrolls of teachings.

wiigwaasabak.name: Wiigwaasabak
wiigwaasabak.summary: A birch bark scroll used by Anishinaabe peoples of North America, inscribed with a geometric writing system to preserve history and, in Midewiwin ceremonies, sacred teachings.

john-clarke-baptist-minister.name: John Clarke
john-clarke-baptist-minister.summary: English-born politician, physician and Puritan Baptist minister (1609–1676), co-founder of Rhode Island and author of its charter, and a leading advocate for religious liberty.

william-coddington.name: William Coddington
william-coddington.summary: Early magistrate of the Massachusetts Bay Colony (c. 1601–1678) who left amid the Antinomian Controversy to help found Portsmouth, Rhode Island, and later became governor of the colony.

roger-williams.name: Roger Williams
roger-williams.summary: English-born minister who founded Providence Plantations in 1636 as a refuge for religious liberty, later becoming Rhode Island; his ideas influenced the First Amendment.

portsmouth-rhode-island.name: Portsmouth, Rhode Island
portsmouth-rhode-island.summary: A town in Newport County founded as one of the four colonies that merged to form Rhode Island and Providence Plantations.

john-bartram.name: John Bartram
john-bartram.summary: American botanist and explorer (1699–1777) based in Philadelphia, called by Linnaeus the greatest natural botanist in the world; started what became the first botanic garden in the US.

philip-syng.name: Philip Syng
philip-syng.summary: A Philadelphia silversmith (1703–1789) who in 1752 made the inkstand later used to sign the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution.

james-bowdoin.name: James Bowdoin
james-bowdoin.summary: An American politician and merchant (1726-1790) who served as governor of Massachusetts and wrote an influential report on the Boston Massacre.

john-adams.name: John Adams
john-adams.summary: Founding Father and second US president (1797–1801), earlier a leader of the American Revolution and the country's first vice president.

john-hancock.name: John Hancock
john-hancock.summary: American Founding Father and merchant, longest-serving president of the Continental Congress and first governor of Massachusetts, whose bold signature on the Declaration of Independence gave rise to 'John Hancock' meaning a signature.

american-academy-of-arts-and-sciences.name: American Academy of Arts and Sciences
american-academy-of-arts-and-sciences.summary: One of the oldest American learned societies, founded in 1780 by John Adams, John Hancock, and other Founding Fathers.
american-academy-of-arts-and-sciences.source_title: American Academy of Arts and Sciences

seven-fires-prophecy.name: Seven Fires prophecy
seven-fires-prophecy.summary: An Anishinaabe prophecy describing seven epochs in the life of the people of Turtle Island, teaching that different peoples can unite in respect; documented in 1988 in The Mishomis Book.

turtle-island.name: Turtle Island
turtle-island.summary: A name some Indigenous peoples of the Americas use for Earth or North America, rooted in an oral history from the Northeastern Woodlands and still used by Indigenous and non-Indigenous activists.

claude-jean-allouez.name: Claude-Jean Allouez
claude-jean-allouez.summary: Jesuit missionary and French explorer (1622–1689) who established several missions among indigenous peoples near Lake Superior.

jacques-marquette.name: Jacques Marquette
jacques-marquette.summary: French Jesuit missionary (1637–1675) who founded Michigan's first European settlement, Sault Sainte Marie, and mapped the northern Mississippi River Valley with Louis Jolliet in 1673.

dakota-people.name: Dakota
dakota-people.summary: A Native American people, one of the main subcultures of the Sioux, traditionally divided into the Eastern Dakota (Santee) and Western Dakota (Yankton and Yanktonai) groups.

christopher-columbus.name: Christopher Columbus
christopher-columbus.summary: Italian explorer and navigator (1451–1506) whose four Spanish-sponsored voyages opened the way for European exploration and colonization of the Americas.

columbian-exchange.name: Columbian exchange
columbian-exchange.summary: The widespread transfer of plants, animals and diseases between the Americas and Afro-Eurasia beginning in the late 15th century, named for Christopher Columbus.

juan-de-o-ate.name: Juan de Oñate
juan-de-o-ate.summary: A Spanish conquistador (1550–1626) who led early expeditions across the Great Plains and founded settlements in New Mexico; notorious for the 1599 massacre at Acoma Pueblo.

daniel-boone.name: Daniel Boone
daniel-boone.summary: American pioneer (1734–1820) who blazed the Wilderness Road into Kentucky in 1775 and founded Boonesborough, becoming an early American folk hero.

transylvania-colony.name: Transylvania Company
transylvania-colony.summary: A land speculation venture led by North Carolina speculator Richard Henderson, whose 1775 purchase of Cherokee land created the short-lived Transylvania Colony in present-day Kentucky and Tennessee.

cumberland-gap.name: Cumberland Gap
cumberland-gap.summary: A mountain pass through the Appalachians near the Kentucky-Virginia-Tennessee border, used by Native Americans and brought to settlers' attention in 1750, later part of Daniel Boone's Wilderness Road.

wilderness-road.name: Wilderness Road
wilderness-road.summary: A steep, narrow 18th-century route through the Cumberland Gap into Kentucky, blazed in 1775 by Daniel Boone for the Transylvania Company and used by thousands of settlers.

sioux.name: Sioux (Oceti Sakowin)
sioux.summary: Groups of Native American tribes from the Great Plains, divided into the Dakota and Lakota peoples, together called the Očhéthi Šakówiŋ, or Seven Council Fires.

ojibwe.name: Ojibwe
ojibwe.summary: An Anishinaabe Indigenous people whose homeland spans the Great Lakes region and northern plains, among the largest Native American and First Nations populations today.

pueblo-revolt.name: Pueblo Revolt
pueblo-revolt.summary: An uprising of Pueblo peoples against Spanish colonists in New Mexico in 1680 that killed 400 Spaniards and drove out the rest, considered the first Native American religious revitalization movement.

cathedral-basilica-of-st-francis-of-assi.name: Saint Francis Cathedral
cathedral-basilica-of-st-francis-of-assi.summary: A Catholic cathedral in Santa Fe, New Mexico, serving as the mother church of the Archdiocese of Santa Fe.
cathedral-basilica-of-st-francis-of-assi.source_title: Cathedral Basilica of St. Francis of Assisi (Santa Fe)

yamasee-war.name: Yamasee War
yamasee-war.summary: 1715–1717 war in the Province of Carolina between British settlers and the Yamasee and allied Native peoples, killing about 7 percent of South Carolina's colonists.

choctaw.name: Choctaw
choctaw.summary: An Indigenous people of the Southeastern Woodlands of the United States, historically based in Louisiana, Mississippi and Alabama, today enrolled in three federally recognized tribes.

muscogee.name: Muscogee (Creek)
muscogee.summary: Group of related Indigenous peoples of the Southeastern Woodlands in the United States, also known as Muscogee Creek, most of whom were forced onto Indian Territory in the 1830s Trail of Tears.

catawba-people.name: Catawba
catawba-people.summary: A Native American tribe along the Catawba River in South Carolina, once among the most powerful in the Southeast, whose numbers fell sharply after colonial contact.

cree.name: Cree
cree.summary: A North American Indigenous people numbering over 350,000, forming one of Canada's largest First Nations groups, with homelands stretching from Quebec across the Canadian Prairies to British Columbia.

black-hills.name: Black Hills
black-hills.summary: A mountain range rising from the Great Plains in western South Dakota and eastern Wyoming, sacred to the Lakota, who took the territory in the 1770s.
